samples.text:
Nowadays, in many countries people can talk to a doctor through a video call on their phone or computer, and they do not need to go to the clinic. I think this is a positive development, but it cannot replace normal visits completely.

The first advantage is that video consultations save time and money. Patients do not need to travel to the clinic or wait for a long time in the waiting room. This is very helpful for people who live in the countryside, where the nearest hospital can be far away. Also, working people do not have to take a whole day off for a short appointment, they can speak with the doctor during their lunch break.

Another advantage is that it reduce the spread of diseases. When sick people sit together in a waiting room, they can easily pass infections to each other. If patients with a cold or a flu stay at home and speak to the doctor online, other patients, specially old people and babies, are more safe.

However, video calls also have some limitation. A doctor cannot examine the patient's body properly through a screen, for example he cannot listen to the heart or check the blood pressure. So there is a risk that some serious illness is missed. In addition, some elderly people do not know how to use video call technology.

In conclusion, I believe that seeing a doctor by video call is a positive development because it is convenient and it can protect people from infections. However, it should be used only for simple problems, and patients should still visit the clinic when they need a physical examination.
samples.why: Clear positive position · relevant ideas with some development · paragraphing logical but linking mechanical · adequate vocabulary · errors including comma splice, agreement, comparative and plural that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In a growing number of countries, patients can now speak to a doctor over a video link rather than attending a clinic in person. In my opinion, this is a positive development, as long as it is used alongside traditional appointments rather than instead of them.

The greatest benefit is improved access to healthcare. For people living in remote areas, a visit to a clinic can involve hours of travel, and for elderly or disabled patients even a short journey may be exhausting. Video consultations allow these groups to receive advice quickly and from the comfort of their own home. They are also convenient for working people and parents, who no longer need to take time off work or arrange childcare for a routine appointment.

Remote consultations can also make health systems more efficient. Many appointments, such as renewing a prescription or discussing test results, do not require a physical examination, and handling them by video frees up clinic space for patients who really need to be seen in person. Furthermore, keeping people with infections out of crowded waiting rooms reduce the risk of illnesses spreading to other vulnerable patients.

Nevertheless, there are clear limitations. A doctor on a screen cannot carry out a full physical examination, and subtle signs of serious illness might be missed. In addition, not every patient has a reliable internet connection or the confidence to use the technology, so an over-reliance on video calls could disadvantage the very people who most need care.

In conclusion, video consultations make healthcare more accessible and efficient, and I therefore see them as a positive development. However, they should complement face-to-face appointments, and patients must always have the option of seeing a doctor in person.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · main ideas well extended with relevant examples · logical organisation and good use of cohesive devices · good collocations (improve access, free up) · mostly error-free with a minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
Consulting a doctor by video call, once a rarity, has become an established part of healthcare in many countries. I view this as a positive development, since it widens access to medical advice and relieves pressure on overstretched clinics, although it works best as a complement to, rather than a substitute for, face-to-face care.

The most important advantage is accessibility. For patients in rural areas, a routine appointment may involve a long journey and considerable expense, while for those with limited mobility or caring responsibilities, simply reaching a surgery can be a significant obstacle. A video consultation removes these barriers, and as a result people may be more willing to seek advice at an early stage rather than delaying until a problem becomes serious.

Remote appointments also allow health services to use their resources more intelligently. A substantial share of consultations, such as reviewing medication or discussing results, require conversation rather than physical contact. Handling these remotely shortens waiting times for patients who do need to be examined and reduces the number of potentially infectious people gathered in waiting rooms.

The limitations, however, should not be underestimated. Certain diagnoses depend on touch, sound and close observation, and a clinician relying on a camera may overlook important signs. There is also a danger that the convenience of video calls leads health providers to cut in-person services, disadvantaging older patients and households without dependable internet access. These risks do not negate the value of remote consultation, but they do mean that its use must be guided by clinical judgement rather than cost-saving alone.

In conclusion, video consultations represent a welcome advance: they bring medical advice within reach of people who previously struggled to obtain it and make better use of limited clinical time. Provided that in-person care remains readily available when needed, this development deserves to be embraced.
samples.why: Clear, qualified positive judgement · well-developed ideas with precise reasoning · limitations integrated into the argument · skilful cohesion · wide, accurate vocabulary · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
